body: Portuguese plates are long and white, with a blue strip on the left. A yellow strip on the right is a unique feature, though it was discontinued in 2020.
The Portuguese language is a Romance language that uses unique letters like Ç, Ã, and Õ. Unlike Spanish, it does not use the letter Ñ.
Eucalyptus trees are very common in Portugal and can also be found in northern Spain.
The Portuguese word for street is 'Rua'.
Concrete ladder poles with very tall steps, often with small holes, are common in Portugal. This distinguishes them from poles in Spain and France which have short steps.
Hunting signs in Portugal have a red and white color scheme. This contrasts with the black and white signs in Spain.
Portuguese bollards can be wedge-shaped or flat and often have white or orange reflectors. The orange is darker than the yellow used in Spain.

Portuguese directional signs are typically white with black arrows that do not touch the border. Spanish signs are different, often using colored boxes for road numbers and lacking a solid black arrow.
Portuguese kilometre markers are wide rectangles with a colored section on the left. Larger square signs with a colored top half appear every kilometer.
Black and white waystones are a common sight in Portugal.
Stop signs in Portugal have a large font, which is a key differentiator from Spanish stop signs that have a small, compact font.
Portuguese chevrons are black with yellow arrows, a unique color combination in the Mediterranean region.
Portuguese pedestrian signs have five stripes and show a person wearing a high belt. This is different from Spanish, Italian, and Greek signs.
Portugal uses A-type guardrails with red reflectors, distinguishing it from Spain which uses yellow reflectors.
Portuguese road signs are typically surrounded by a white border, unlike most Spanish signs.
Cobblestone roads made of square stones arranged diagonally are very common in Portugal.
Cobblestone sidewalks made of bright stones are also very common in Portugal.
White painted stone houses with orange tiled roofs are extremely common in Portugal.
Houses often have blue or yellow lines painted around windows, doors, and wall edges.
Houses decorated with mosaic tiles (Azulejos) are a feature of Portuguese architecture.
Portugal has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, recognizable by its lower position and large circular blur, which can sometimes be transparent.
In the southern Faro district, look for decorative chimneys, with round chimneys being a particularly strong clue.
In northern Portugal, houses are often made of square concrete blocks joined with white mortar. This helps distinguish them from similar houses in Galicia, Spain.
The southeast features open fields with small holm and cork oaks, creating a landscape known as Montado.
Olive plantations, identified by trees planted in dense rows, are common in the eastern half of Portugal.
Dense eucalyptus forests are a key feature of the northwest region.
Maritime pine forests are common in the northern half of Portugal. These trees have grey bark with red undertones and upward-pointing branches.
The Douro wine region, east of Porto, is known for its steep terraced vineyards.
Citrus plantations are primarily found along the south coast.
The islands of Madeira and the Azores are part of Portugal and have their own distinct features.
The Serra da Estrela natural park is recognizable by its rocky, mountainous landscape and yellow and black striped snow poles.
Pine forests with extremely sandy white soil are a clue for the coastal area between Setúbal and Sines.
The far southwest is a flat, uncultivated, and dry landscape with very limited vegetation like low bushes and grass.
Lime green street signs are a unique feature of the city of Porto.
